title: Total Gaussian Curvature
notes: Open with the central balance law rather than a list of definitions. The chapter asks how a curve drawn on a surface can read both the curvature inside the region and the topology of the region. The visible loop should be read as a measuring device: boundary turning, interior Gaussian curvature, and corner angles all contribute to one accounting identity.

title: Lecture Route
notes: Use the route slide to orient the audience before formulas arrive. Each stop has a different measurement target. A surface curve separates ambient bending from intrinsic turning, Gauss-Bonnet converts local curvature into a global ledger, parallel transport measures a returned angle, and holonomy turns small loops into curvature probes.

title: Surface Curves Have Two Curvatures
notes: Pause on the decomposition of acceleration. A curve on a surface can bend because the surface itself bends in space, and it can also turn within the surface. The first contribution is normal curvature and depends on the embedding direction. The second is geodesic curvature and is the boundary term that Gauss-Bonnet will integrate.

title: Boundary Turning Lives In The Tangent Plane
notes: This slide reframes geodesic curvature as a steering rate. The tangent vector is constrained to remain in the tangent plane of the surface, and the Levi-Civita connection tells how much of its change is intrinsic turning. Corners are not swept under the rug; their exterior angles are added as discrete turning events.

title: Gauss-Bonnet Is A Ledger
notes: Present the formula as bookkeeping. The interior term measures Gaussian curvature across the region, the boundary term measures intrinsic turning along the boundary, and the corner sum records jumps in tangent direction. Their total is not arbitrary; it lands on two pi times the Euler characteristic of the region.

title: Two Calibration Regions
notes: Use the flat disk and the spherical triangle as calibration examples. In the Euclidean disk the curvature term vanishes, so all of the two pi comes from boundary turning. On the sphere, a geodesic triangle has zero geodesic curvature along the sides, so the angle excess is paid for by the curved interior.

title: Hemisphere Check
notes: The hemisphere is the cleanest mental test. The boundary equator is a geodesic, so its geodesic curvature term vanishes. The region is a disk, so the right side is two pi. Therefore the total Gaussian curvature over the unit hemisphere must supply exactly two pi.

title: Annulus Cancellation
notes: The annulus teaches orientation discipline. In the flat plane the Gaussian curvature is zero, and the Euler characteristic of an annulus is zero. The outer boundary and the inner boundary are oriented in opposite ways, so their geodesic curvature contributions cancel rather than add.

title: Parallel Transport Around A Loop
notes: Move from boundary turning to transport. A tangent vector is carried along the curve by asking its covariant derivative in the curve direction to vanish. The equation preserves vector length and inner products, but after a closed loop the returned vector may be rotated relative to the initial one.

title: Holonomy Detects Enclosed Curvature
notes: This slide makes the local meaning of holonomy explicit. For a small loop, the returned angle is approximately the integral of Gaussian curvature over the enclosed patch, with sign determined by orientation. Positive curvature behaves like a tiny rotation source, while flat regions produce no first-order angle defect.

title: Why Topology Appears
notes: Explain the topological term through cancellation. When a region is triangulated, edge contributions appear twice with opposite orientations and disappear in pairs. What remains is the angle bookkeeping at vertices and the count of faces, edges, and vertices, which is exactly where the Euler characteristic enters.

title: Notebook Diagnostics
notes: Tie the lecture to the assigned notebook artifacts. The numerical checks are not decorative; they protect the identities from visual guesswork. The notebook tests orthonormal frame preservation, hemisphere total curvature, flat annulus cancellation, and the preservation of tangent-vector length under transport.

title: Common Misreads
notes: Use this slide as a guardrail before the recap. Students often mix normal curvature with geodesic curvature, forget that boundary orientation changes signs, ignore corner angles, or treat holonomy as an arbitrary rotation. Each mistake breaks a different term in the Gauss-Bonnet accounting identity.

title: Recap: Curvature Becomes Accounting
notes: Close by tracing the dependency chain. Curves on surfaces provide geodesic curvature. Regions collect Gaussian curvature. Corners and orientations complete the boundary record. Gauss-Bonnet converts those measurements into topology, while holonomy gives a transport-based way to sense the same curvature locally.
